card.stem: The sketch shows portion of the eaves of a pitched roof constructed using prefabricated trussed rafters. The roof is supported on a 400 mm concrete block wall with a full-fill insulated cavity. The roof has a pitch of 30° and the trussed rafters are 200 mm × 40 mm. The slates are fixed to 50 mm × 30 mm battens, on a breather membrane. The roof is highly insulated at ceiling joist level.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:5, draw a vertical section through the external wall of the house and through the eaves of the trussed roof. On your drawing, show the typical construction details from a level 400 mm below the wallplate, through the wall and eaves of the roof. Include the first three courses of slate at eaves. Include three typical dimensions on your drawing.

rows.contextNote: Any 7 x 5 marks. Credit the best SEVEN acceptable details at 5 marks each, capped at 35. Marked details: concrete block outer leaf with external render; full-fill cavity with wall tie; concrete block inner leaf with internal plaster; cavity closer; wallplate 100 mm × 75 mm; prefabricated roof truss; insulation and airtight membrane; plasterboard with skim coat; fascia, soffit and gutter; ventilation; breather membrane; slates and battens. The model specifies 19 mm render, 100 mm leaves, a 200 mm full-fill cavity, 15 mm plaster, a tilting fillet and 50 × 30 mm battens.

options: Concrete block outer leaf with external render
Full fill cavity with wall tie
Concrete block inner leaf with internal plaster

rows.contextNote: Three appropriate typical dimensions on the section.

rows.verbatim: Draughting, accuracy and scale (excellent, good, fair)
rows.contextNote: Draughting, accuracy and scale of the section: excellent 8, good 6, fair 4.

card.stem: New homeowners wish to improve the Building Energy Rating (BER) of their home which was built over 30 years ago. The external wall is a concrete block wall with a partially insulated cavity. It is proposed to fix insulation to the inside surface of the external walls, and to install new windows.
card.questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show one suitable method of applying insulation to the internal surface of the walls. Show on your sketch how the wall is to be finished internally. Specify the type and thickness of insulation.

rows.verbatim: Method of insulating external walls note & sketch (8 + 8 marks)
rows.contextNote: Note 8 and sketch 8 of one method, showing the internal finish. Such as: clean the wall of wallpaper or gloss paint, cut insulated plasterboard to size and fix it with mechanical fixings (adhesive dabs may also be used), then skim with plaster or tape and fill; or fix timber battens to the wall, fill between them with insulation, then fix plasterboard to the battens and skim.

rows.verbatim: Preferred insulation type for external wall
rows.contextNote: Such as: expanded polystyrene (EPS), phenolic, polyisocyanurate (PIR) or extruded polystyrene (XPS); the method notes also name wood fibre and sheep’s wool.
At least 50 mm of insulation.

card.questionText: Explain, with the aid of notes and freehand sketches, any five of the following: site planning notice; halving joint; faceplate turning; smart lighting; cordless drill; plywood; gulley trap; cavity closer; heat pump.

rows.contextNote: Explain any five of the nine terms. Each term is marked separately: primary communication of relevant information 6 and other communication 4, in notes or sketches (the scheme reserves no fixed split between them). Site planning notice: a public notice the applicant erects at the site when applying for planning permission, clearly visible and legible from the road, giving the applicant’s name, site address, type of application and nature of the development; required by planning regulations so the public can make observations or objections; in place for the first five weeks after lodgement, or the application may be invalid. Halving joint: a common, strong woodworking joint with a medium gluing area, made by removing half the material from each piece at the joint; cross, corner, T- or dovetail halving; used in framing and furniture. Faceplate turning: a woodturning method for large, flat circular items such as bowls and plates; the work piece is mounted on a faceplate on the headstock of the lathe; the tool rest supports the chisel; start slowly until the piece is balanced, then increase the speed. Smart lighting: lighting controlled remotely, often automatically, through a smartphone, tablet or voice commands over the internet; scheduling and timers; customised colour, brightness and ambiance; contributes to energy savings. Cordless drill: a portable power tool for drilling holes and driving screws, powered by rechargeable (usually lithium-ion) batteries; more convenient and versatile than a corded drill and usable where there is no power source; features such as an LED light and battery indicator. Plywood: an engineered panel of thin wood veneers glued with the grain of each layer perpendicular to the next for strength; used in construction, furniture and cabinet-making; a strong, relatively low-cost alternative to solid wood; marine plywood for high-moisture use. Gulley trap: a fitting in foul and rainwater drainage with a U-bend that holds water as a seal against sewer gases and odours entering the building; typically underground; needs regular maintenance. Cavity closer: closes the gap between the leaves of a cavity wall at wallplate level and around window and door openings; prevents thermal bridging, damp penetration, air infiltration and condensation; insulating foam or rigid board, 100–150 mm wide to suit the cavity. Heat pump: a device transferring heat from the air, water or ground into the home, distributed by underfloor heating or radiators; runs on electricity with a coefficient of performance of about 3–4; grants encourage the change from fossil-fuel heating.
